title: What does Norfolk's Zoning Ordinance say about opening a restaurant in a Ghent building?
summary: General rules from the City's official Zoning Ordinance: when a restaurant needs a Conditional Use Permit (alcohol, late hours, under 80% seating, entertainment), who decides it, the Certificate of Appropriateness for exterior changes in the Ghent historic districts, the Zoning Certificate any change of use needs and how it expires, the Certificate of Occupancy, the limits on accessory structures and accessory uses (plumbing, floor area), and when a small restaurant in an older building in the Downtown, Traditional or Coastal character districts needs no parking. It does not say which district a given address is in, whether a restaurant is allowed there (the use table differs by district), or how a particular carriage house would be classified; those need the zoning map and a zoning determination for the address.

what_would_help.text: If the restaurant will serve alcohol, plan for a Conditional Use Permit and its public hearing before opening.
Before changing the building's exterior, apply for a Certificate of Appropriateness.
Before changing what a building is used for, get a Zoning Certificate from the Zoning Administrator.

pending: Which Ghent district (HC-G1, HC-G2, HC-G3 or a commercial district) a given address is in: Norfolk AIR (the City's GIS viewer) and the City's Zoning layer of its Planning map service show the district for each address; read it from there, then use Table 3.6.11 for that district.

Whether a restaurant is allowed in that district: Table 3.6.11 (Historic and Cultural Conservation districts) shows restaurant as permitted-or-conditional (P/C) in HC-G3 and not permitted in HC-G1 or HC-G2 by the page image; a column-in-a-table cell can't be quoted exactly, so it is not a finding yet.

Rules for converting a carriage house to a commercial use: the ordinance sections read name carriage houses only for the R-C (Ocean View) district and in flood-plain definitions. The general limits on accessory structures (plumbing) and accessory uses (25 percent of floor area) are findings; whether a given carriage house would be an accessory structure or could hold a principal use is a Zoning Administrator's determination (§2.4.17) for the address.

Whether the Ghent districts (HC-G1, HC-G2, HC-G3) are in the Traditional character district, which the small-restaurant parking exemption (§5.1.2) turns on: each district's dimensional table is headed "Traditional Character District" in the page image, but a table header can't be quoted as a statement, and the character district boundaries are on the Official Zoning Map.

What counts as a "pre-existing building" and how occupant load is set for the small-restaurant parking exemption (§5.1.2): the ordinance sections read don't define either; occupant load is a Building Code figure.
